product.title: Spanish 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Spanish: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Spanish builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. From greeting people to telling the story of what happened yesterday.

blocks.text: Most people don't give up on Spanish because the language is hard, but because they lose their way: vocabulary piles up without ever being used, and grammar rules arrive before the ear has had time to get used to the sounds.

This course turns that habit upside down. Each unit starts with a conversation you can use right away — ordering a coffee, saying how old you are, asking for directions — and only afterwards explains why the sentences are built the way they are. The explanations are deliberately short. What's long isn't the theory; it's the practice.

The twenty short units inside cover everything at **Level A1 (CEFR)**: introductions, where you're from, family, numbers, time, daily routines, places, shopping, plans, and telling the story of yesterday. Work through them in order without skipping the exercises, and by the end you'll be able to hold your own in simple everyday conversations.
One thing no book can replace: someone to talk to. Use this course to prepare the material, then look for chances to use it with real people.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours in bits and pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read out loud. Spanish is pronounced almost exactly as it's written, and your mouth remembers what your eyes forget.
Keep a small notebook. Words you write down last far longer than words you only read.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *¡Buena suerte!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Diálogo** — first read the Spanish out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears do the work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it's where you see how Spanish *thinks*. Example: *Me llamo Ana* literally means "myself I call Ana", not "my name is Ana".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Spanish, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Spanish sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Spanish spelling is far more honest than English — almost every letter is read just as it's written. Reading silently throws that advantage away.
The good news: Spanish is written the way it sounds. Once you know the table below, you can read any word correctly — including words you've never seen before.

head: Letter
Sounds like
Example
rows: **ah, eh, ee, oh, oo** — always short and crisp, never gliding (*o* is not "oh-w", *e* is not "ay")
a breathy **h** from the back of the throat
r at the start of a word, rr

blocks.title: Word stress
items: Words ending in a **vowel, -n or -s** → stress on the **second-to-last** syllable: *CA-sa*, *HA-blan*, *LI-bros*.
Words ending in any other consonant → stress on the **last** syllable: *ha-BLAR*, *ciu-DAD*.
A written accent (*é*, *á*) → the stress falls exactly there, no exceptions: *ca-FÉ*, *MÉ-di-co*. The mark isn't decoration.

blocks.text: In this course, the "Say it" column is written for English readers, and **capital letters mark the stressed syllable**: **BWEH-nahs TAHR-dehs** = *buenas tardes*. Vowels are always **ah, eh, ee, oh, oo**; vowel pairs are written **eye** (*hay* → eye), **ay** (*seis* → says), **oy** (*hoy* → oy), **ow** (*autobús* → ow-toh-BOOS); an *i* or *u* before another vowel becomes **y** or **w** (*adiós* → ah-DYOHS, *bueno* → BWEH-noh). Consonants: **h** = Spanish *j* and *g* before e/i (the written *h* is silent and simply left out); **y** = *ll* and *y*; **ny** = *ñ*; **k** = *qu* and hard *c*; **s** = *z* and *c* before e/i (Latin American pronunciation); **b** = *v*; **g** is always hard (*seguir* → seh-GEER); a single **r** stays r, **rr** is the long rolled r.
Everything from the twenty units, condensed into a few pages. This section isn't meant to be read in order — it's for coming back to whenever you hesitate mid-sentence.
Nouns and articles
The exceptions that trip people up most: *el día* (masculine), *la mano* (feminine), *el agua* (feminine but takes *el*), *el mapa*, *el problema*, *el idioma* (all masculine despite ending in -a).
Adjectives

items: They go **after** the noun: *una camisa blanca*.
They agree in gender and number: *alto / alta / altos / altas*. Those ending in -e or a consonant only change in the plural: *grande → grandes*, *azul → azules*.
Comparing: *más … que* (more … than), *menos … que* (less … than), *tan … como* (as … as).
Four have their own forms: *bueno → mejor*, *malo → peor*, *grande → mayor*, *pequeño → menor*.

blocks.text: Possessives and demonstratives
Verbs — present tense

blocks.title: Ser, estar, hay
items: **ser** — identity, origin, permanent qualities, time, price, ownership, where an **event** takes place.
**estar** — where things are, temporary states, feelings, open/closed.
**hay** — "there is / there are"; never changes form, always with *un / una / dos / muchos*, never with *el / la*.

blocks.text: Stem-changing verbs
The *nosotros* and *vosotros* forms **never** change — that's the hallmark of this whole group: *queremos*, *podemos*, *pedimos*.
Verbs — past tense
Future, obligation, ability

items: **ir a + infinitive** — plans ("going to"): *voy a estudiar*.
**tener que + infinitive** — personal obligation ("have to"): *tengo que trabajar*.
**hay que + infinitive** — general obligation ("one has to"): *hay que pagar aquí*.
**poder + infinitive** — can / may: *¿puedo probarlo?*
**querer + infinitive** — to want to: *quiero descansar*.

blocks.text: The gustar pattern
Same pattern: *encantar* (to love), *apetecer* (to feel like), *doler* (to hurt), *interesar* (to interest), *parecer* (to seem), *quedar* (to fit, of clothes).
Commands

head: tú (informal)
usted (polite)
Negative (tú)
rows: ven, haz, ve, pon, sal, ten, di, sé
venga, haga, vaya, ponga, salga, tenga, diga, sea
no vengas, no hagas, no vayas

blocks.text: Numbers
Time

items: Clock: *Es la una* · *Son las tres y cuarto* · *Son las cuatro menos veinte* · *Son las ocho y media*.
Days: *lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo* — lowercase. *el lunes* = this Monday; *los lunes* = every Monday.
Months: *enero, febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre* — also lowercase.
Dates: *el quince de mayo*. Past: *ayer*, *anoche*, *la semana pasada*, *hace dos días* (two days ago).

blocks.text: Small words that change a sentence

head: Word
Meaning
Notes
rows: *a + el* → **al**; before a person as object: *veo a Marta*

blocks.text: These forty verbs cover most A1 conversations. The last column is the past-tense *yo* form — the one you'll reach for most when telling a story.

blocks.title: How to use this table
items: Don't memorize it in order. Pick the five verbs you need most this week, cover the right-hand columns, and say the forms out loud until they come out without a pause.
If a form feels unfamiliar, find the verb in the unit where it first appeared — the sentence around it sticks far better than a list.
The *nosotros* form is deliberately left out: you can almost always build it yourself by adding **-mos** to a pattern you already know.

blocks.text: If you've finished every unit and can do the wave reviews without looking at the key, you're on the threshold of **A2**: you can introduce yourself, ask and answer everyday questions, order things, and talk briefly about your routine.
Three things that will raise your level fastest from here:

items: **Talk to people.** Reading a course trains understanding; only conversation trains speed. Linguo's private classes with native-speaker teachers are designed for exactly that.
**Listen every day, even for 10 minutes.** Songs, beginner podcasts, or Spanish-language series with Spanish subtitles — not English ones.
**Write five sentences a day** about your day. Short is fine; what you're training is the habit of building sentences, not their length.
